content: 1. When filling a spray tank, it is essential to minimize the amount of foam produced. This requirement applies to all formulations that are diluted with water before use. Persistent foam should not exceed 60 mL after one minute. The test should use the maximum recommended application rate of the product. Persistent foaming is not tested after storage at elevated temperatures for formulations in water-soluble bags, as surfactants are unlikely to become more effective after storage. 2. For ultra-low volume (UL) formulations, it is critical to ensure that rapid evaporation of sprayed droplets does not lead to unacceptable drift. Volatility testing methods are not standardized, and the evaporation rate depends on droplet size, composition, and air temperature. The initial droplet size is influenced by the application equipment. Any method used for volatility testing must be submitted to FAO/WHO with supporting data to validate its accuracy. 3. Flash point is a key safety characteristic of many liquid formulations. Under the FAO/WHO guidelines, flash point limits were previously included but have been withdrawn in the new procedure. Flash point is determined by the solvents used in the formulation and is controlled during manufacturing. It is a measure of hazard, not performance, and its risks depend on the specific application and climate. National registration authorities assess these risks, as global specifications for flash point are challenging to establish. If flash point is a significant concern, a note may be added to specifications to emphasize adherence to national requirements. 4. The wet sieve test aims to limit the content of insoluble particles that could block sprayer nozzles or filters. This test applies to various formulations, including wettable powders, suspension concentrates, water-dispersible granules, and others. A typical requirement is that no more than 2% of the sample is retained on a 75 µm sieve. 5. The dry sieve test is used to restrict unwanted particle sizes in powders and granules intended for direct application or seed treatment. General limits cannot be provided, as they depend on the specific product. 6. Ensuring an acceptable proportion of granules within a nominal size range minimizes segregation during transport and handling, ensuring uniform flow rates through application equipment. At least 85% of the formulation should fall within the nominal size range. Particle size may affect biological activity and application equipment suitability. 7. Dustiness of granular formulations must be restricted to reduce risks to users during handling and application. Dustiness can be measured using gravimetric or optical methods, with the gravimetric method serving as the referee in case of disputes. 8. Granular and tablet formulations must resist attrition to remain intact during handling and transport, minimizing dust generation and ensuring field efficacy. Attrition resistance is often related to packaging design. Testing methods include MT 178 for granules and MT 193 for tablet friability. 9. Tablet integrity must be maintained to ensure the intended dose is applied. No broken tablets should be present in at least one package containing multiple tablets. Visual observation is the standard method for this assessment. 10. Adhesion to seeds is critical for seed treatment formulations to ensure the intended dose remains on the seeds and is not easily removed. This minimizes handling risks and ensures efficacy. General limits cannot be provided. 11. Particle size range in suspensions must be sufficiently narrow to ensure optimal efficacy and safety. This applies to multi-phase formulations, with limits being product-dependent. 12. Tablet hardness must ensure that tablets remain intact during handling and application. No suitable test methods are currently available, and limits are product-dependent. 13. Dispersibility and spontaneity of dispersion ensure that formulations rapidly and easily disperse when diluted with water. For suspension concentrates and capsule suspensions, at least 60% of the active ingredient should remain in dispersion. For water-dispersible granules, dispersibility should be at least 60% by gravimetric analysis. 14. Disintegration time and dispersibility/dissolution ensure that soluble or dispersible tablets disintegrate rapidly in water, allowing the formulation to disperse or dissolve effectively. 15. Suspensibility ensures that a sufficient amount of active ingredient is homogeneously dispersed in the spray liquid to provide an effective mixture during spraying. At least 60% of the active ingredient should remain in suspension for wettable powders, suspension concentrates, and similar formulations. 16. Dispersion stability ensures that the active ingredient remains homogeneously dispersed in suspension or emulsion throughout spraying. Testing should be conducted at the highest and lowest recommended use rates. 17. Emulsion stability and re-emulsification ensure that the active ingredient is uniformly dispersed in the emulsion, providing an effective mixture during spraying. Tests are typically conducted before and after heat stability testing. 18. Flowability ensures that granules for direct application flow freely from application machinery and that granules for dispersion or dissolution in water do not clump after storage. General limits cannot be provided. 19. Pourability ensures that formulations can be easily poured from containers. The maximum residue remaining in the test cylinder should not exceed 5%. The test does not define the pouring and rinsing characteristics of containers, which are unique to each formulation/container combination. 20. Viscosity testing ensures that ultra-low volume (UL) formulations have suitable viscosity properties for their intended purpose. Limits are product-dependent, and methods include rotational viscometry and kinematic viscosity testing. 21. Acidity, alkalinity, or pH range must be controlled to prevent decomposition of the active ingredient, deterioration of physical properties, or container corrosion. Acidity and alkalinity should be expressed as g/kg H₂SO₄ and NaOH, respectively. General limits cannot be provided.
